issues.legal_issue: A plaint in a specific-performance suit may be amended to add an omitted readiness-and-willingness averment when the amendment completes the existing claim without causing irremediable prejudice.
material_facts: The plaintiff sued to enforce an agreement to sell property, alleging part payment and possession, after the defendant failed to execute the sale deed following receipt of the required permission.
The original plaint did not specifically allege that the plaintiff was and had always been ready and willing to perform his part of the agreement.
The defendant objected that the suit was not maintainable, and that issue was set for preliminary determination.

The plaintiff sought to amend the plaint to add the readiness-and-willingness averment; the trial court rejected the request, and the High Court upheld that decision because the request was made after limitation and would disturb a vested right.
The proposed amendment added no new cause of action and was intended to complete the existing claim for specific performance.
issues.conclusion: The appeal was allowed, the lower courts' orders were set aside, and the amendment was permitted.
issues.legal_principle: Under Order VI Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure, amendments necessary to determine the real questions in controversy should generally be allowed if they do not work injustice to the other side. An amendment should be refused where the other party would suffer an injury that cannot be compensated in costs. The possibility that a fresh suit on an amended claim would be time-barred is a factor in exercising discretion, not a limit on the court's power to allow an amendment in the interests of justice. Here, the amendment merely completed the existing cause of action by adding the averment required by Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, and introduced no fresh cause of action. The Court relied on Pirgonda Hongonda Patil v. Kalgonda Shidgonda Patil and L.J. Leach & Co. v. Jardine Skinner & Co., and distinguished Ouseph Varghese v. Joseph Aley, where a decree had been granted on an agreement different from the one pleaded by the plaintiff.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and amendment_application_pending and amendment_needed_for_real_controversy and opponent_would_suffer_no_irremediable_injury and (not fresh_suit_on_amended_claim_time_barred or amendment_adds_no_new_cause_of_action)

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The plaintiff brought a suit seeking enforcement of an agreement to sell property.
predicates.amendment_application_pending: The plaintiff applied to amend the plaint while the suit was pending.
predicates.amendment_needed_for_real_controversy: The proposed amendment supplied an omitted averment needed to complete the plaintiff's existing claim.
predicates.opponent_would_suffer_no_irremediable_in: The amendment would not cause the opposing party an injury that could not be compensated or otherwise addressed.
predicates.fresh_suit_on_amended_claim_time_barred: A fresh suit asserting the claim in the proposed amended form would be barred by limitation when the amendment was sought.
predicates.amendment_adds_no_new_cause_of_action: The proposed amendment did not introduce a cause of action different from the one already pleaded.

issues.definition: When an amendment in a pending specific-performance suit is needed to resolve the existing claim and causes no irremediable injury, it may be permitted even if a fresh suit on the amended claim would be time-barred, provided the amendment adds no new cause of action.
